coach_says: Your f6 knight is pinned to your queen by Bg5, Nd5 is piling on it, and the d7 knight is what holds everything together. b6 does nothing about that, so Bb5 hits d7 and when it goes, your queen on d8 falls to Bxd8. When a piece is pinned to your queen, deal with the pin first: free the queen or make a counter-threat (Re8 sets up ...Nxe4), instead of a quiet pawn move.

Your c6 knight was the only thing guarding e5. Moving it to d4 just leaves the pawn, and Nxe5 also lines the knight up with Bc4 against f7, threatening Nxf7 forking your queen and rook. Before moving a piece, check what it was defending; d5 or h6 keep e5 covered and fight for the centre.

White's knight on f3 is attacking your e5 pawn, and Bc5 doesn't defend it, so Nxe5 simply wins a pawn. After 2.Nf3 your first job is to protect e5 (Nc6 or d6) or counter-attack with Nf6. Each time the opponent moves, ask what the new move attacks.

Your bishop on b5 was attacked by the c6 pawn, and your two knights were only holding each other up against h6 and Bf5. Qh5 doesn't save the bishop, and after hxg5 the h-file opens onto your queen, so you lose a piece. When you are ahead in material and several pieces are under fire, first save the loose piece: Bd3 rescues the bishop and guards e4.

Your bishop on d3 has no safe squares: c4 can be hit by a pawn, and its retreat via e2 is blocked by your own queen and the d2 pawn hems it in. After Re1, ...c4 just traps it and wins a piece for a pawn. Keep an escape route for your pieces: b3 meets ...c4 with bxc4, or move the queen so e2 is free.

Black's last move, Ne6, attacked your bishop on f4, and nothing was defending it. Bb3 ignores that, so Nxf4 wins a piece for free. After every opponent move, ask what it attacks; here Be5 or Bg3 keep the bishop safe and still active.

Rd7 set up Qf7 mate: the rook supports the queen on f7 and your king has nowhere to go. Taking on h2 ignores that and loses at once. When the opponent's queen and rook combine near your king, check for mate before grabbing anything; Qg6 covers f7 and keeps you in the game.

You had two ways to block the check, and the rook was the wrong blocker. On g7 the rook was guarding the seventh rank and the squares around your king; once it goes to g8, Qf6+ and Re7+ crash in and it is mate. When you block a check, ask what the blocking piece was doing before; Bg8 keeps the rook on guard and holds a draw.
concept: blocked check with the wrong piece

coach_says: When you recapture, look at what each piece is guarding. Your queen was the only defender of the knight on e7, which the rook on e4 was attacking. After Qxc8, Rxe7 wins the knight; Nxc8 recaptures with the attacked piece itself and keeps material level.

White's g4 push is meant to open lines against your king, and g5 helps them: it loosens the squares around your king and gives White an easy h4 to rip the h-file open. When your opponent advances pawns at your castled king, leave your own king pawns alone and hit back elsewhere, here with ...b5 on the queenside or by improving the d7 knight.

f6 opens the diagonal from c4 to your king, so White's bishop arrives with check and gains time. Meanwhile your knight on d4 gets kicked by c3, and its natural retreat to b3 fails because Bc4+ comes first and then the bishop takes it. In the endgame, bring your rooks to the open files (Rfb8, Rab8) rather than making pawn moves near your king.
concept: opened the diagonal to your king

coach_says: Your king is still in the middle and Black's bishop on h6 controls the dark squares c1, d2 and e3. Nc3 develops but lets Black's queen jump to g5 or h4, attacking f2 together with the rook on f7 and threatening Qd2. A pawn on h4 shuts the queen out of g5 and h4 and makes the rest of your development safe.

With pawns on e6 and g6, your dark-squared bishop is what guards the holes on f6 and h6. Bh6 offers to swap it straight away, and after Bxh6 Nxh6 your knight sits on the edge and those dark squares stay weak for the whole game. Keep that bishop (Bg7) and play d6 to fight for the centre.

Your f4 pawn was attacked by the bishop on c1 and the g3 pawn. Pushing it to f3 doesn't save it: Nxf3 takes it and develops White's knight at the same time. A better answer is Bh6, which defends f4 and gets your own piece out.
concept: pawn push that helps opponent develop

coach_says: Your f3 knight is pinned to your queen by the bishop on h5. gxf6 lets Black's queen recapture on f6 and pile on f3, so you have to scramble to avoid losing material. Sort out a pin before you open lines: Nbd2 or Bxc6+ and then Nbd2 adds a defender to f3, and the g5 pawn can wait.

Black's knight on f6 is the only defender of the d5 pawn. Bxf6 removes it, and after Qxf6 Nxd5 you win a second pawn with tempo on the queen. Retreating with Bg3 gives Black time for Qb4 hitting b2. When a piece is guarding something, ask whether you can capture the guard.

Black's last move, b5, left that pawn unprotected, and your bishop on f1 could just take it. a4 misses that and also takes away the a3 pawn's protection of b4, so Black's knight grabs it instead. Before pushing a pawn, check what it was defending, and look for free material after every opponent move.
concept: missed a free pawn on b5

coach_says: d5 is about as good as anything here; you are already a couple of pawns down and the engine's choices are all close. Just keep your pieces coordinated and look for chances against White's advanced pawns.
Qd3 is fine, close to the engine's best. Still, moving your queen for the third time costs development; getting the knights out and playing c4 or g3 would make your setup work better.

Your queen is lost to Bxd1 whatever you do, so take what you can: Rxh2 grabs the knight that just gave check, and you can still recapture on d1 afterwards. After Ke1 the knight escapes via f3 and you end up a whole piece worse. When you're losing material anyway, look for what of theirs you can take in return.
